assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 'Credit Cycles' showed how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, giving a dynamic general-equilibrium account of credit-driven fluctuations. It is the core of modern macro-financial models and has shaped analysis of the 2008 crisis, policy design and later quantitative work. The model has a clear mechanism and a long record of extension.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the originators of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial-accelerator line (with Bernanke). Bernanke and Gertler's work was partly recognised in 2022, so I limit the proposal to the two originators of the collateral-price feedback.
assessment.maturity: The paper is nearly three decades old and thoroughly tested, theoretically and empirically, including during the 2007-09 crisis. Timing is ripe, with no sign of a recent challenge.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize (banks and financial crises) may weigh against recognising a closely related theme.
Whether Gertler and Gilchrist should be included to reflect the financial-accelerator tradition is a judgement on boundaries.
My assessment relies on general knowledge, not independently verified sources.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz's 2003 model of firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed how trade is theorised and measured. It put productivity differences across firms at the centre and explained gains from trade through reallocation. Helpman's work on trade with monopolistic competition and firm-level models, with Krugman and others, extended the 'new trade theory' framework. The area has wide empirical and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the heterogeneous-firm model. Helpman is a long-standing foundational contributor who helped build the new trade theory and the firm-level extensions. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covered the earlier new trade theory, and Redding's quantitative work is more recent and derivative.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets and countries, with the framework now standard in graduate teaching and policy analysis.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize overlaps with Helpman's earlier contributions, so the incremental case needs weighing.
Whether Redding should be added for quantitative implementation, or whether this dilutes the core discovery.
Quantitative trade models in the same period (see B046) may compete for the same prize slot.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi documented, with granular data and credible identification, that household leverage and credit supply expansions drive booms and subsequent busts in consumption and employment. This gave empirical content to debt-overhang and demand-side channels of crises, and it reshaped debate on mortgage credit, monetary and fiscal policy.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the leading and consistent co-authors of this programme, from housing and household balance sheets to the 'credit-driven household demand channel'. Campbell has important work on household finance and mortgages, but he is not central to the macroeconomic credit-boom discovery.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from about 2009 to 2015, and has been replicated and extended in many countries. Recognition is likely sooner than for the very youngest candidates, but a longer track record would strengthen the case.
uncertainties: Some findings, such as the extent of credit supply versus other drivers, remain debated.
Distinctiveness relative to the 2022 prize on financial crises is uncertain.
Relative timing compared with older foundational theory candidates is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Sticky-price models (Calvo), policy-rule analysis (Taylor) and the micro-founded New Keynesian framework (Woodford and others) underpin how central banks think about inflation targeting and stabilisation. The impact on practice is large, and the tools are the workhorse of macro-policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: The field is a collective achievement with many contributors, including Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans and Smets-Wouters. Three names must stand for it, which is a real compromise. Calvo supplied time-dependent pricing, Taylor the rule, and Woodford the integrated normative theory. The selection leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. The framework has been used and debated for decades, including after the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation episode.
uncertainties: Attribution is the main difficulty: many contributors and the three-name limit make any allocation contestable.
Doubts about the framework's performance during the financial crisis and inflation surge may influence assessment.
Partial overlap with earlier prizes in macroeconomics (rational expectations, DSGE and policy rules).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the 'China shock' evidence showed how automation and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets, polarisation and political outcomes. The work is empirically careful and highly influential on both academic and public policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the central authors of the trade-shock evidence. Autor also anchors the task-based labour-demand framework. Katz belongs to the earlier skill-biased technical change tradition and Goldin was recognised in 2023, while Acemoglu's 2024 prize and related task-based work reduce the unique contribution somewhat.
assessment.maturity: The key evidence is about a decade old, with ongoing follow-up on long-run effects. It is reasonably mature, but long-run interpretations are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Acemoglu's 2024 prize and Goldin's 2023 prize.
Debate about how far the China shock results generalise, and about identification and long-run persistence.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for further evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's 1982 alternating-offers bargaining model is a foundation of modern bargaining theory, with a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium and a transparent link between patience and division. With Wolinsky it was extended to decentralised markets, which links to search and matching. The influence on theory and applied modelling (labour, trade, political economy) is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator. Wolinsky is credited for the market-bargaining extensions. Binmore contributed key bridging and interpretation, and Stahl's earlier related result is a point of attribution. Nash and Selten/Harsanyi earlier recognitions cover adjacent game theory.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, having been in the core of microeconomic theory for four decades with extensive follow-on work.
uncertainties: Whether the committee still favours game-theory recognition after the 2020 and earlier game-theory prizes.
Attribution regarding Stahl and Binmore, and the allocation among theoretical versus market applications.
Empirical and policy influence is more indirect than for macro and applied candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Dasgupta-Heal work on optimal depletion of exhaustible resources, and later work on inclusive wealth and the economics of biodiversity, anchors the theory of sustainability and natural capital. It shaped how resources and ecosystems enter growth and welfare accounting. It also complements the Nordhaus (2018) recognition, covering natural capital and resource stocks instead of climate damages.
assessment.attribution: Dasgupta and Heal developed the capital-theoretic resource models jointly, and Dasgupta led the inclusive-wealth and biodiversity extensions. Solow, Stiglitz and Hotelling had earlier foundational contributions in this area. The field overlaps with my own research area (climate-economy modelling), so I note this as a disclosed proximity and apply common criteria.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work is from the 1970s and well established. The inclusive-wealth and biodiversity parts are more recent and have had less empirical and practical confirmation.
uncertainties: Practical influence of inclusive wealth on measurement and policy is still developing.
Overlap with the 2018 prize, and with Solow, Stiglitz and Hotelling lineage.
Possible concern about my field proximity and the possibility of overrating work close to my own interests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) offered a tractable framework quantifying how misallocation of inputs across firms lowers aggregate productivity, accounting for part of cross-country income gaps. It created a large empirical literature on frictions and productivity in development and macroeconomics, and it links micro data to aggregate outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the authors of the canonical measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson's closely related contribution on policy distortions is also important. Restuccia is credited here, and the question of how to share credit for the idea is genuinely open.
assessment.maturity: About 15 years of influence. The approach is widely adopted, but the interpretation of measured wedges and measurement error is still debated, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Measured 'misallocation' may partly reflect measurement error or unobserved heterogeneity.
Credit division with Restuccia and Rogerson.
Possible overlap with the 2025 growth prize and with earlier growth and development recognitions.
